GSAP entrance animation runs once per view switch on visible cards only, honors reduced-motion. Fonts lazy via unicode-range. - **IPC payloads**: `StoredLibraryCard` already drops body/metadata fat for the wire; `getItemContent`/`getItem` are narrow per-item detail reads. ## Top 3 for the next two days 1. **Slim the embedding-scan query** (finding 1). It fixes keystroke-search stalls *and* most of the Smart Space cost in one place, it's ~20 lines in `search.ts` + mirrored in `searchSimilar`, no schema or IPC change, and it composes with any future ANN work. Highest certainty of user-visible pain once the library has real content. 2. **Slim `itemColumns` for card reads** (finding 2). Fixes startup→first-cards and every reload/patch read. It's the same "load fat, throw it away" class as #1 and ships as one column-list change in `shared.ts` plus the `has_article_content` flag. Slightly more plumbing, still small. 3. **Warm the query ONNX session after storage opens** (finding 3). One line of fire-and-forget in `openStorage`; removes the "first search hangs for seconds" first-run impression — cheap insurance for alpha week. Do #4 (edge-blur layers 5→2) only after `bench-library-grid` says scrolling is actually janky; same for touching LiquidGlass. ## Confidence High confidence in the top two findings — the code reads are unambiguous and they hit the exact slow paths named in the product principles (typing, first paint). Classic scroll-jank pattern on Windows; magnitude is GPU-dependent — `scripts/bench-library-grid.mjs` already exists to measure. - **Fix:** `layers: 5 → 2` halves the passes with minimal visual change; or replace blur with an opacity fade (bigger visual change, dev's call). - **Effort:** S. **Risk:** medium — it's a deliberate visual treatment; needs design sign-off if reduced. **5. Whole grid lives inside a `layoutsubtree` canvas when WebGPU is available — `SUSPECTED`** `LibraryStage.tsx:44-47` wraps the grid in `LiquidGlass`; `LiquidGlass.tsx:402-405, 414` moves `children` into a `liquid-glass-content` div painted inside a `h-screen w-screen` WebGPU canvas, and `WebGpuDomContentSource` copies the painted grid to texture on each `paint` event (`draw`, lines 285-321). Idle cost is zero (paint-event driven, line 282), and `.glass` targets are bounded (toolbar chrome + video-card pills + tooltips — LibraryCard.tsx:158 is video-only), so this may be fine on decent GPUs. Up to 8MB responses (line 31) → ~100-500ms event-loop stall per captured article → all IPC (and thus the renderer) hitches while the user keeps browsing. Bounded and one-shot per capture. - **Fix:** smallest is capping `rawHtml` bytes before parse (~2-3MB covers real articles); the honest fix for "background work never blocks browsing" is a `worker_threads` wrapper around `ingestUrl`. - **Effort:** S (cap) / M (worker). **Risk:** low. **8. Fresh image cards render the original file until the thumbnail lands — `SUSPECTED`** `libraryItem.ts:161-164`: `item.thumbnailPath ?? (kind === "Image" ? item.localAssetPath : null)` → grid `` is the untouched original (up to 50MB, `items.ts:201`) until `image_thumbnail` completes. Storage opens lazily on first IPC via `initializeLibraryStorage` single-flight (main.ts:235-244); models, OCR worker, ONNX sessions all defer to first job/query (embeddings.ts:217-245, ocr.ts:36-53). `show:false` + `ready-to-show` + 3s fallback (main.ts:441,473-477). Migrations are one-time-sync `openDatabase` work (schema.ts:197-235); FTS rebuild only on version/count mismatch (schema.ts:182-188). - **Capture ordering** — insert + `jobs.enqueue` in one transaction, nothing awaits enrichment/OCR/embedding/thumbnail: items.ts:122-131 (URL), 139-147 (note), 170-178 (quote), 221-245 (file). `saveFile` only reads image *headers* (items.ts:205-208). Renderer paths all persist-then-render (useCapture.ts:47-54, 98-108, 223-229, 265-272). - **Job queue**: serial per worker with a separate thumbnail worker so new-card thumbnails never queue behind OCR/embeddings (main.ts:206-217, ai-jobs.ts:265-267). PubSub wakeup + 5s fallback poll, leases, heartbeat, interrupt-releases (worker.ts:76-92, jobs.ts). Heavy compute is off the main thread: Tesseract worker, ONNX `session.run`, sharp. `SILENT_JOB_KINDS` keeps thumbnail/palette/poster out of renderer traffic. - **Renderer data path**: memo'd `LibraryCard` (293), `patchItems` preserves identity for unchanged cards, job events coalesce 400ms, `total_changes()` probe polls only when visible (30s), virtualized masonry grid, images `loading="lazy" decoding="async"` + `fetchPriority` only on first 6, `assetUrl` is pure string math (no IPC per asset), asset protocol streams files with Range support (asset-response.ts). - **Mascot**: single shared engine, rAF only while subscribed + visible + not reduced-motion (mascotStore.tsx:56-90). GSAP entrance animation runs once per view switch on visible cards only, honors reduced-motion. Fonts lazy via unicode-range. - **IPC payloads**: `StoredLibraryCard` already drops body/metadata fat for the wire; `getItemContent`/`getItem` are narrow per-item detail reads. ## Top 3 for the next two days 1. **Slim the embedding-scan query** (finding 1). It fixes keystroke-search stalls *and* most of the Smart Space cost in one place, it's ~20 lines in `search.ts` + mirrored in `searchSimilar`, no schema or IPC change, and it composes with any future ANN work. Highest certainty of user-visible pain once the library has real content. 2. **Slim `itemColumns` for card reads** (finding 2). Fixes startup→first-cards and every reload/patch read. input.body:
Read-only audit done (Devin SWE-2, max). I checked the top two claims against the code and both hold.

Ranked findings:

1. **Semantic search scans every embedding row with full item columns** (`electron/storage/search.ts:102`, same shape in `searchSimilar` and Smart Spaces). Reads and JSON.parses `ocr_text` + `metadata` (article html/text) for every embedded item on each debounced search, on the main-process event loop. CONFIRMED. Fix: select only `item_id, dimension, vector`, score, take top-K, then load cards for those ids. Effort S.
2. **Card queries load `ocr_text` + full `metadata` per row, then discard them** (`shared.ts` `itemColumns`, `cardItem` keeps 180 chars of OCR and a few metadata fields). Hits startup to first cards and every reload. CONFIRMED. Fix: card-only projection (`substr(ocr_text,1,220)`, `json_remove(...)`, a `has_article_content` flag). Effort M.
3. **First search after boot blocks on ONNX session creation.** SUSPECTED. Fix: fire-and-forget query-embedding warmup after storage opens. Effort S.
4. Ten stacked backdrop-filter layers over the scrolling grid (`LibraryEdgeFade`). SUSPECTED, measure first.
5. Grid painted inside the WebGPU liquid-glass canvas. SUSPECTED, measure first.
6. Open Smart Space re-embeds its query on every load (mostly fixed by 1). CONFIRMED.
7. URL enrichment parses fetched HTML 3x on the main thread. SUSPECTED.
8. Fresh image cards render the original file until the thumbnail lands. SUSPECTED.

Checked and fine: startup order, capture ordering, job queue isolation, renderer data path, mascot loop, lazy chunks, IPC payloads.

Proposed fix order: 1, 2, 3. Runtime baseline still open (bench ported to Windows, click step fails against the glass layer).

input.task:
You are fixing one performance problem in inkling (Electron + React + SQLite, Windows). Read AGENTS.md at the repo root first and follow it. It is strict about scope, comments, tests, and safety.

## Problem
In `electron/storage/search.ts`, semantic search (`searchItems`, around lines 99-123) and `searchSimilar` (around lines 125-154) scan every embedding row but select the full item columns (`qualifiedItemColumns`, which include `ocr_text` and `metadata`, and metadata holds the whole article html/text). For every debounced search keystroke, the main process reads and JSON.parses every embedded item's OCR text and article metadata, only to dot-product a vector and then discard almost everything. This runs on the Electron main-process event loop, so all IPC stalls with library size. The same scan is reached by Smart Spaces (`electron/storage/spaces.ts` around line 202).

## Required fix
Score using only the lightweight columns (`e.item_id`, `e.dimension`, `e.vector`, joined to `items` just for the archived/kind filters). Pick the top results by score (respecting the existing cap and tie-break by updatedAt where the current code uses it), and only THEN load full card rows for the winning ids, restoring score order. Lexical (FTS) matches must keep their existing behavior: they still get the `score: 2` seeding and merge exactly as today. No schema, index, IPC contract, or renderer change.

Note: updatedAt is used as a tie-break in `searchItems`, so the lightweight scan needs `i.updated_at` too (or you must justify another way of keeping the identical ordering). Behavior, result set, and order must stay identical to today for every input.

## How to prove it (this repo wants this)
1. First write characterization tests against the CURRENT implementation, extending the existing storage test file(s) (`electron/storage.test.ts` and any helper in `electron/storage/test-library.ts`; extend before you add). They must pass on the unmodified code. Cover: semantic-only matches above the match floor, lexical+semantic merged ranking and score, the result cap, archived items excluded, wrong-dimension or wrong-model embeddings skipped, `searchSimilar` ordering and its kind filter, and the source item excluded. Keep the number of tests small; do not write tests the types already prove, no timing or perf assertions, no fixed sleeps.
2. Then refactor. The same tests must still pass.
3. Run only `bun test <the files you touched>` while iterating and `bun run check:changed` at the end. Do NOT run the full test suite or `bun run check`. Run `bun install --frozen-lockfile --ignore-scripts` first if node_modules is missing.

## Hard rules
- Do not launch the app, Electron, or any dev server. Do not touch any real user library. Never kill processes by name or pattern.
- Do not open a PR and do not push. Do not edit docs/changelog.md or any docs; the reviewer will do that.
- Default to no comments. Only add one where a reader would break something without it (an ordering or invariant), one line.
- Effect 4 is used in this directory and differs from Effect 3. Before writing Effect code read `node_modules/effect/AGENTS.md` and `node_modules/effect/ai-docs/`. Reusable functions use `Effect.fnUntraced`.
- Commit your work on the current branch with a conventional title such as `perf(search): score embeddings without loading full items`.

## Final report
Reply with: the files changed, a short summary of the diff, the names of the tests you wrote and confirmation they passed before AND after the refactor, the `check:changed` output summary, and anything you were unsure about or chose not to do.

input.title: SQU-15 fix 1: slim embedding scan (Devin medium)
input.task:
You are fixing one performance problem in inkling (Electron + React + SQLite, Windows). Read AGENTS.md at the repo root first and follow it. It is strict about scope, comments, tests, and safety.

## Problem
In `electron/storage/search.ts`, semantic search (`searchItems`, around lines 99-123) and `searchSimilar` (around lines 125-154) scan every embedding row but select the full item columns (`qualifiedItemColumns`, which include `ocr_text` and `metadata`, and metadata holds the whole article html/text). For every debounced search keystroke, the main process reads and JSON.parses every embedded item's OCR text and article metadata, only to dot-product a vector and then discard almost everything. This runs on the Electron main-process event loop, so all IPC stalls with library size. The same scan is reached by Smart Spaces (`electron/storage/spaces.ts` around line 202).

## Required fix
Score using only the lightweight columns (`e.item_id`, `e.dimension`, `e.vector`, joined to `items` just for the archived/kind filters). Pick the top results by score (respecting the existing cap and tie-break by updatedAt where the current code uses it), and only THEN load full card rows for the winning ids, restoring score order. Lexical (FTS) matches must keep their existing behavior: they still get the `score: 2` seeding and merge exactly as today. No schema, index, IPC contract, or renderer change.

Note: updatedAt is used as a tie-break in `searchItems`, so the lightweight scan needs `i.updated_at` too (or you must justify another way of keeping the identical ordering). Behavior, result set, and order must stay identical to today for every input.

Keep the number of tests small; do not write tests the types already prove, no timing or perf assertions, no fixed sleeps.

input.title: SQU-15 fix 2: card-only column projection (Devin high)
input.task:
You are fixing one performance problem in inkling (Electron + React + SQLite, Windows). Read AGENTS.md at the repo root first and follow it. It is strict about scope, comments, tests, and safety.

## Problem
Card reads in the main process load far more than a card needs. `electron/storage/shared.ts` defines `itemColumns` / `qualifiedItemColumns` which include the whole `ocr_text` and the whole `metadata` JSON (metadata holds article `html`, `text`, `extractedText`, `safeEmbeds`, `imageDimensions`). `listActiveItems` in `electron/storage/items.ts` (around line 369) calls `selectCards(ctx, sql`archived = 0`)` with no LIMIT, and other card reads (search results, Space listings, patch reads) go through the same columns. `cardItem` in shared.ts then discards almost all of it: it keeps `ocrText` trimmed and sliced to 180 chars, a fixed allowlist of metadata fields (`cardMetadataFields`), and computes `hasArticleContent` from `metadata.html`. So startup to first cards and every reload pay for reading and JSON.parsing the whole article corpus, on the main-process event loop.

## Required fix
Add a card-only projection used by card reads: truncate `ocr_text` in SQL, strip the heavy metadata keys in SQL (e.g. `json_remove(metadata, '$.html', '$.text', '$.extractedText', '$.safeEmbeds', ...)`), and compute `hasArticleContent` in SQL so `cardItem`/`cardFromRow` can use it. Keep `detailColumns` / `getItem` behavior unchanged. The output of every card read must be byte-for-byte identical to today for every input.

Edge cases you MUST handle, they are the whole risk of this change:
- Malformed or non-object metadata JSON. Today `parseJson` falls back to `{}` silently. SQLite's `json_remove` and `json_extract` ERROR on malformed JSON, which would fail the entire list query for the whole library. Guard with `json_valid(...)`, or an equivalent that degrades per row, and test it.
- `hasArticleContent` today is `typeof metadata.html === "string" && metadata.html.trim() !== ""`. Reproduce that exactly (whitespace-only html, non-string html, missing html).
- `ocrText` today is `String(ocr_text ?? "").trim().slice(0, 180)`. Truncating in SQL must not change the result, including when the text starts with lots of whitespace, so choose the SQL truncation length/approach carefully and say why in your report.
- The projection must keep working for every caller of `selectCards`, `cardFromRow`, and the search/Space paths that reuse the columns. Find them all with grep and decide per caller; do not break `searchItems`/`searchSimilar`, which another change is rewriting in `search.ts`, so keep your edits in `shared.ts`/`items.ts`/`context.ts`/callers minimal and avoid reformatting `search.ts`.

## How to prove it
1. First write characterization tests against the CURRENT implementation, extending `electron/storage.test.ts` / `electron/storage/test-library.ts` (extend before you add). They must pass on unmodified code. Cover: card output for items with large html/text metadata, whitespace-only and non-string html, leading-whitespace and very long OCR text, malformed metadata JSON, and that the card allowlisted metadata fields (tags, social, imageUrls, imageDimensions, mediaWidth, mediaHeight, mediaAspectRatio, pdfPageCount) still come through. Keep the number of tests small; no timing or perf assertions, no fixed sleeps.
2. Then implement. The same tests must still pass.

input.title: SQU-15 fix 3: warm query ONNX session (Devin medium)
input.task:
You are fixing one performance problem in inkling (Electron + React + SQLite, Windows). Read AGENTS.md at the repo root first and follow it. It is strict about scope, comments, tests, and safety.

## Problem
The first search (or first Smart Space open) after app boot stalls for seconds. `search_items` in `electron/main.ts` (around lines 297-299) calls `embedQueryForSearch`, which reaches `electron/embeddings.ts` (around line 234) `textQueryRuntimePromise ??= openTextRuntime(false)`, which creates an ONNX `InferenceSession` over the roughly 500 MB Nomic model plus the tokenizer JSON. That cost lands on the first keystroke, before the FTS query even runs. Later queries are fast.

## Required fix
After storage has opened successfully in `electron/main.ts` (see `openStorage` / `initializeLibraryStorage` around lines 228-244), fire-and-forget a warmup of the query embedding runtime (for example `ai.embedQuery("warmup")`) so the session and tokenizer are created during idle time. Constraints, all important:
- It must never block startup, window show, or capture, and a failure must be swallowed (search already falls back to lexical-only when the embedding returns null).
- It must NOT trigger a model download. Local-first rule: the network is only used for the one-time model download the user asked for. Verify by reading `electron/embeddings.ts` that the warmup path only uses models already on disk and does nothing, quietly, when they are missing. If the existing query path could download, do not warm up through it; find or add the narrowest path that cannot, and say so in your report.
- It should run once per app launch, not on every storage open or reload.
- Keep the diff tiny. Do not restructure anything.

## How to prove it
Add or extend a test only if it guards something that breaks quietly (for example: warmup failure is swallowed and does not reject, or warmup does not start a model download when models are absent). Use the existing electron tests (`electron/embeddings.test.ts`, `electron/ai-jobs-lazy.test.ts`) as the model, extend before you add, no fixed sleeps, no timing asserts. If no test earns its place, say why in your report. Run only `bun test <the files you touched>` while iterating and `bun run check:changed` at the end. Do NOT run the full test suite or `bun run check`. Run `bun install --frozen-lockfile --ignore-scripts` first if node_modules is missing.

## Hard rules
- Do not launch the app, Electron, or any dev server. Do not touch any real user library or model cache. Never kill processes by name or pattern. Never hardcode an absolute path or port.
- Do not open a PR and do not push. Do not edit docs/changelog.md or any docs; the reviewer will do that.
- Default to no comments. Only add one where a reader would break something without it, one line.
- Effect 4 is used in `electron/` and differs from Effect 3. Before writing Effect code read `node_modules/effect/AGENTS.md` and `node_modules/effect/ai-docs/`.
- Commit your work on the current branch with a conventional title such as `perf(search): warm the query embedding model after storage opens`.

## Final report
Reply with: the files changed, a short summary of the diff, the tests (or why none), the `check:changed` output summary, and what you verified about downloads and failure handling.

input.title: SQU-15 fix 1: slim embedding scan (Devin high)
input.task:
You are fixing one performance problem in inkling (Electron + React + SQLite, Windows). Read AGENTS.md at the repo root first and follow it. It is strict about scope, comments, tests, and safety.

## Problem
In `electron/storage/search.ts`, semantic search (`searchItems`, around lines 99-123) and `searchSimilar` (around lines 125-154) scan every embedding row but select the full item columns (`qualifiedItemColumns`, which include `ocr_text` and `metadata`, and metadata holds the whole article html/text). For every debounced search keystroke, the main process reads and JSON.parses every embedded item's OCR text and article metadata, only to dot-product a vector and then discard almost everything. This runs on the Electron main-process event loop, so all IPC stalls with library size. The same scan is reached by Smart Spaces (`electron/storage/spaces.ts` around line 202).

## Required fix
Score using only the lightweight columns (`e.item_id`, `e.dimension`, `e.vector`, joined to `items` just for the archived/kind filters). Pick the top results by score (respecting the existing cap and tie-break by updatedAt where the current code uses it), and only THEN load full card rows for the winning ids, restoring score order. Lexical (FTS) matches must keep their existing behavior: they still get the `score: 2` seeding and merge exactly as today. No schema, index, IPC contract, or renderer change.

Note: updatedAt is used as a tie-break in `searchItems`, so the lightweight scan needs `i.updated_at` too (or you must justify another way of keeping the identical ordering). Behavior, result set, and order must stay identical to today for every input.

## How to prove it (this repo wants this)
1. First write characterization tests against the CURRENT implementation, extending the existing storage test file(s) (`electron/storage.test.ts` and any helper in `electron/storage/test-library.ts`; extend before you add). They must pass on the unmodified code. Cover: semantic-only matches above the match floor, lexical+semantic merged ranking and score, the result cap, archived items excluded, wrong-dimension or wrong-model embeddings skipped, `searchSimilar` ordering and its kind filter, and the source item excluded. Keep the number of tests small; do not write tests the types already prove, no timing or perf assertions, no fixed sleeps.
2. Then refactor. The same tests must still pass.
3. Run only `bun test <the files you touched>` while iterating and `bun run check:changed` at the end. Do NOT run the full test suite or `bun run check`. Run `bun install --frozen-lockfile --ignore-scripts` first if node_modules is missing.

- Do not open a PR and do not push. Do not edit docs/changelog.md or any docs; the reviewer will do that.

input.title: SQU-15 fix 2: card-only column projection (Devin high)
input.task:
You are fixing one performance problem in inkling (Electron + React + SQLite, Windows). Read AGENTS.md at the repo root first and follow it. It is strict about scope, comments, tests, and safety.

## Problem
Card reads in the main process load far more than a card needs. `electron/storage/shared.ts` defines `itemColumns` / `qualifiedItemColumns` which include the whole `ocr_text` and the whole `metadata` JSON (metadata holds article `html`, `text`, `extractedText`, `safeEmbeds`, `imageDimensions`). `listActiveItems` in `electron/storage/items.ts` (around line 369) calls `selectCards(ctx, sql`archived = 0`)` with no LIMIT, and other card reads (search results, Space listings, patch reads) go through the same columns. `cardItem` in shared.ts then discards almost all of it: it keeps `ocrText` trimmed and sliced to 180 chars, a fixed allowlist of metadata fields (`cardMetadataFields`), and computes `hasArticleContent` from `metadata.html`. So startup to first cards and every reload pay for reading and JSON.parsing the whole article corpus, on the main-process event loop.

## Required fix
Add a card-only projection used by card reads: truncate `ocr_text` in SQL, strip the heavy metadata keys in SQL (e.g. `json_remove(metadata, '$.html', '$.text', '$.extractedText', '$.safeEmbeds', ...)`), and compute `hasArticleContent` in SQL so `cardItem`/`cardFromRow` can use it. Keep `detailColumns` / `getItem` behavior unchanged. The output of every card read must be byte-for-byte identical to today for every input.

Edge cases you MUST handle, they are the whole risk of this change:
- Malformed or non-object metadata JSON. Today `parseJson` falls back to `{}` silently. SQLite's `json_remove` and `json_extract` ERROR on malformed JSON, which would fail the entire list query for the whole library. Guard with `json_valid(...)`, or an equivalent that degrades per row, and test it.
- `hasArticleContent` today is `typeof metadata.html === "string" && metadata.html.trim() !== ""`. Reproduce that exactly (whitespace-only html, non-string html, missing html).
- `ocrText` today is `String(ocr_text ?? "").trim().slice(0, 180)`. Truncating in SQL must not change the result, including when the text starts with lots of whitespace, so choose the SQL truncation length/approach carefully and say why in your report.
- The projection must keep working for every caller of `selectCards`, `cardFromRow`, and the search/Space paths that reuse the columns. Find them all with grep and decide per caller; do not break `searchItems`/`searchSimilar`, which another change is rewriting in `search.ts`, so keep your edits in `shared.ts`/`items.ts`/`context.ts`/callers minimal and avoid reformatting `search.ts`.

## How to prove it
1. First write characterization tests against the CURRENT implementation, extending `electron/storage.test.ts` / `electron/storage/test-library.ts` (extend before you add). They must pass on unmodified code. Cover: card output for items with large html/text metadata, whitespace-only and non-string html, leading-whitespace and very long OCR text, malformed metadata JSON, and that the card allowlisted metadata fields (tags, social, imageUrls, imageDimensions, mediaWidth, mediaHeight, mediaAspectRatio, pdfPageCount) still come through. Keep the number of tests small; no timing or perf assertions, no fixed sleeps.
2. Then implement. The same tests must still pass.
3. Run only `bun test <the files you touched>` while iterating and `bun run check:changed` at the end. Do NOT run the full test suite or `bun run check`. Run `bun install --frozen-lockfile --ignore-scripts` first if node_modules is missing.

- It must never block startup, window show, or capture, and a failure must be swallowed (search already falls back to lexical-only when the embedding returns null).
- It must NOT trigger a model download. Local-first rule: the network is only used for the one-time model download the user asked for. Verify by reading `electron/embeddings.ts` that the warmup path only uses models already on disk and does nothing, quietly, when they are missing. Run D (fix #3 at Devin medium) is correct and tiny, but I want one adjustment before merging. Run C (fix #2) is still going.

## Run D review
- **Diff:** `electron/main.ts` only, +10/−1. After storage opens it fires `void embedQueryForSearch("warmup")` once per launch.
- **Failure handling:** `embedQueryForSearch` already swallows every error into `null`, so the warmup can't reject, block, or break search.

Devin traced the path to `ensureAsset(..., allowDownload=false)`, and the existing `embeddings.test.ts` row ("text-query embeddings do not download model assets during search") already guards that. Declining to add a test is the right call under your test rules.

## My concern
Storage opens when the renderer calls `initialize_storage` at boot, so the warmup would fire at the same moment the first library list loads. Creating an ONNX session over a roughly 500 MB model is heavy disk and CPU work, and it could slow startup to first card. That is the thing this whole pass is meant to protect. I haven't measured it, so I can't say how much.

A small tweak fixes this: start the warmup a few seconds after storage opens, using a plain timer, instead of immediately. The first search would still be fast, and the first card would not wait on the model. I'd make that change when merging, as one line.

| Fix #1 | High run chosen (`t3/search-embedding-scan-perf`) |
| Fix #3 | Accepted with the delay tweak (`t3/warm-query-embedding-on-boot`) |

- **ocrText**: two traps handled. (a) SQLite `trim()` strips ASCII spaces only, so the trim uses an explicit `char(...)` set matching `String.prototype.trim` (incl. `\u00a0`, `\u3000`, `\ufeff` — the test pins this). question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

This tool runs Git Bash (POSIX sh), not cmd.exe or PowerShell. Use Unix shell syntax: `/dev/null` not `NUL`, forward slashes, `$VAR` not `%VAR%` or `$env:VAR`. Do not use PowerShell here-strings (`@'…'@`) or backtick continuation here — for multi-line strings use a heredoc.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `find`, `grep`, `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background. With it, `timeout` limits how long the command may run in the background before it is stopped (default 1800000 ms, max 7200000 ms).

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: Glob
tools.description: Fast file pattern matching. Supports glob patterns like "**/*.js" or "src/**/*.ts". Returns matching file paths sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: The glob pattern to match files against

path.description: The directory to search in. If not specified, the current working directory will be used. IMPORTANT: Omit this field to use the default directory. DO NOT enter "undefined" or "null" - simply omit it for the default behavior. Must be a valid directory path if provided.

tools.name: Grep
tools.description:
Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: ListAgents
tools.description: Lists agents you can SendMessage to — in-process subagents you spawned, the teammates on your team, other local Claude sessions on this machine, your Claude sessions running in the cloud (when this session has cloud access; a cloud session receives your message but cannot message any session back yet — do not ask it to reply, read its answer in its own transcript), and (when Remote Control is connected here) your account's other sessions — Remote Control sessions on other machines and cloud sessions, each row labeled by kind. Names are the address: send with `SendMessage({to: "<name>", message: "..."})`, copying the name exactly as a row prints it. Append a row's ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — two rows share it, or an error asks you to disambiguate.

channel.description: Not available in this build; leave unset.

q.description: Not available in this build; leave unset.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. With `run_in_background` the timeout is instead how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000ms / 30 minutes, max 7200000ms / 2 hours); at that limit it is stopped and you are notified.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice.

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background. With it, `timeout` limits how long the command may run in the background before it is stopped (default 1800000 ms, max 7200000 ms).

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

level.description: Effort level the review ran at

findings.description: Verified findings, most-severe first; empty if none survived

file.description: Repo-relative path of the file the finding is in

short_summary.description: Compressed label for compact UI (≤60 chars): the claim alone, no rationale or consequence clause

category.description: Short kebab-case slug of the finding type, e.g. "correctness", "simplification", "efficiency", "test-coverage"

verdict.description: Set when a verify pass ran; absent on inline-only reviews

outcome.description: Set ONLY when re-reporting after applying fixes: what happened to this finding

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

args.description: Optional arguments for the skill

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>

The first numbers are too noisy to trust yet:

- The run against fix #2's worktree is still going. It was slow enough to run past the 10-minute foreground limit, which is a warning sign for that SQL projection.

I'll wait for it to finish, then rerun base and fix #2 back to back so they are comparable. I'll report numbers, not impressions.

Two things I've already confirmed about run C:
- **SQLite engine:** SQLite is 3.53.4 in both Electron's Node and Bun, so the JSON functions behave the same in tests and in production.
- **Callers:** every card-producing caller in the diff now reads the card columns. I found no path where `cardItem` loses its `.trim()` on a full row.

I have one suspicion to test. The projection evaluates the `json_each` subquery per row, and for a lexical search matching many items SQLite may evaluate it for every match before applying the `LIMIT`. That would make fix #2 slower for broad searches, not faster.

The results look noisy—C's numbers come out fastest, but A's lexical run also seems suspiciously fast compared to base, likely due to cold cache or machine load rather than real performance differences. I should rerun these tests back-to-back in the same session for a fair comparison, since the absolute timing values seem unexpectedly large.

SearchSimilar stays around 600-740ms consistently across variants, which suggests the bottleneck isn't the schema changes but something else entirely—maybe decoding 2000 vectors of 768 floats each, or moving large blobs through the SQL client. I want to check decodeFloatVector and dotProduct after getting cleaner timing data, but I need to scale down the test (fewer samples, fewer items) since a full rerun would take too long.

Comparing like-for-like: base's listActive is probably noisy/cold since A's identical code only took 0.67s versus the reported 9.9s for base, so the real improvement from C is maybe only 14%, not 17x. Lexical search looks much more promising though — roughly 2.7x faster going from A to C — and hybrid search improves similarly, though I need to test with A, C, and D all merged together to see the combined effect since that hasn't been measured yet. My plan is to cherry-pick these changes onto the branch and rerun the benchmark against a clean base, though I need to figure out how to isolate a clean base given my uncommitted bench changes.

Rather than setting up a fresh worktree, which would require reinstalling node_modules, I'll just integrate directly in C's existing worktree that already has dependencies installed. I'll cherry-pick A's commit onto C's branch there, resolve the conflicts in search.ts between A's rewritten column handling and C's swapped column constants, and build the integrated commit that way before bringing it over to the main branch.

content.thinking:
Looking at CPU time improvements with combined approach versus baseline for 1000 items at 40kB: listActiveItems speeds up 2.6x, lexical search 2.9x, hybrid 2.0x, and similarity search 1.7x. I should note that process.cpuUsage measures across all threads in the process, so this includes the synchronous node:sqlite work happening on the main thread alongside the Effect runtime.

Checking the min-max ranges confirms no overlap between baseline and combined across all four operations, so these gains look statistically solid rather than noise. Still, 359ms to list 1000 items remains a real cost that blocks the main thread -- this is a meaningful improvement but not a true fix; the deeper solution would mean moving html/text into a separate table, which is a bigger migration. I also notice listActiveItems lacks a LIMIT clause, and searchSimilar's 219ms for 1000 vectors works out to 0.2ms per vector, which points to decodeFloatVector as a likely bottleneck worth investigating next.

content.text: CPU time shows a consistent improvement. Next I'm checking why vector scoring still costs about 0.2 ms per item.

# Changelog

All notable development phases and changes are recorded here. See also [roadmap.md](roadmap.md) for what comes next.

The best times to update this file so as to minimize friction while working with a developer or contributor are:
1. When completing a medium-large implementation pass of features, bug fixes, performance enhancements, refactoring updates, or likewise changes
2. The user indicates, whether directly or indirectly through their actions, they want to or are going to finish up the local work and merge the changes afterwards
3. Before starting a new, unrelated task — close out the entry for the work just finished rather than letting it blur or get jumbled into the next thing
4. When a change alters public behavior: API contracts, CLI flags, config options, env vars; anything a user of the project depends on being stable

Changelog entry format: 

- Follow [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/): group entries under `Added`, `Changed`, `Fixed`, `Removed`, `Deprecated`, `Security`.
- Each entry is one line, written for a human reader — what changed in simple technical terms that someone could understand with simple google searches, not a commit message or file diff summary.
- Reference issue/PR numbers or ticket IDs when they exist
- Keep an `Unreleased` section at the top; move entries under a version heading at release time

Guardrails:
- Never mention that changes were made by an AI agent or even a developer — write entries as if the changes were just made
- Don't editorialize or pad entries to look more substantial than the change was
- If a change is trivial (typo fix, formatting, comment-only), skip the changelog — not every commit needs an entry
- Ask before rewriting or reordering existing changelog history when you notice it is drifting from the required structure; only append.
- When restructuring this document NO important/crucial/technical details should be lost



## Unreleased

### Added

- Right-click a card to read, open its link, copy its link, show it in its folder, or archive it, from a menu in the library's glass (#170)
- Buttons show a short label on hover or keyboard focus, in the same glass as the controls around them (#170)
- Settings → General → Open source licenses lists every shipped dependency, vendored component, and bundled model with its license text and source, searchable and filterable by license (#170)
- Settings → Appearance switches components between alternative looks while we compare them, the grid/list toggle as the current pill or a coss ui segmented control, and the sidebar button as buttons in the sidebar header and toolbar or a grip on the library frame's edge (#170)
- Ctrl+\ (⌘+\ on a Mac) shows or hides the sidebar (#170)
- First-run welcome flow on first launch of the installed app, replayable from Settings → General
- PDF cards now show page-one thumbnails generated in the background after capture; existing PDFs are backfilled one at a time when the job queue is idle.
- Chrome MV3 extension saves a page or right-clicked link through inkling's local capture receiver, with the existing capture link as fallback.
- `bun run ui:smoke` drives the core library flows in Electron against a scratch profile and fails on console errors
- Electron desktop shell alongside Tauri, with scoped `app://` assets, an IPC command allowlist, and `inkling://` capture links.

input.body:
Three audit fixes are committed on `squidlee/squ-15-perf-pass-and-bundle-size-baseline` (no PR yet):

* `perf(library): read only card fields for card queries`
* `perf(search): score embeddings without loading full items`
* `perf(search): warm the query embedding model after storage opens` (delayed 5s so it never competes with the first cards)

Measured on a scratch library of 1,000 articles with ~40 kB html each, main-process CPU time per call (wall-clock was useless, another build was saturating the machine). Base then after:

* listActiveItems 937 ms to 359 ms
* searchItems lexical 2078 ms to 718 ms
* searchItems hybrid (semantic) 1782 ms to 875 ms
* searchSimilar 375 ms to 219 ms

Base min/max and after min/max do not overlap for any of the four. Synthetic data, so the ratio is the finding, not the absolute numbers.

What is still slow: the whole items row is still read from disk (html lives in `items.metadata`), and `decodeFloatVector` builds a boxed JS array per 768-float vector (~0.2 ms each). Next candidates: decode into a Float32Array view, then consider moving article html/text out of the items row.

Still open: runtime startup baseline (bench click step blocked by the glass layer intercepting clicks, waiting on the fix PR), edge-blur and WebGPU glass costs, URL enrichment HTML parsing on the main thread, fresh image cards showing the original until the thumbnail lands.

content.text:
Fixes #1, #2 and #3 are committed on `squidlee/squ-15-perf-pass-and-bundle-size-baseline`. I haven't made a PR. `check:changed` passes: oxlint, oxfmt, 42 storage tests, knip and typecheck.

## Measured effect
This is main-process CPU time per call on a synthetic library of 1,000 articles with about 40 kB of HTML each. I used CPU time because wall-clock was useless: a `rustc` build of something else was saturating the machine.

| Call | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `listActiveItems` | 937 ms | 359 ms |
| Lexical search | 2,078 ms | 718 ms |
| Hybrid (semantic) search | 1,782 ms | 875 ms |
| `searchSimilar` | 375 ms | 219 ms |

Before and after ranges don't overlap on any of the four, so the 2–3× improvement is real. The data is synthetic and the machine was loaded, so trust the ratio more than the milliseconds.

## What the Devin trial showed
- **Fix #1, high vs medium:** same solution. High had better tests (the `updatedAt` tie-break, the image branch) and simpler code, so I merged high.
- **Fix #2, high:** this was the hard one. It handled the malformed-JSON trap, JS-versus-SQLite trim differences, and the `hasArticleContent` rule. It declined to fix an unrelated pre-existing bug in `taggedItemIds` and flagged it instead. That is the right call.
- **Fix #3, medium:** correct and tiny. I added a 5-second delay so the model load doesn't compete with the first cards.
- **Fix #2 interaction:** fix #2 also edits `search.ts`, so merging the two needed a hand-resolved conflict. I did that and all 42 tests pass.

## Still slow, so next
- **Vector decoding:** it builds a boxed JS array of 768 numbers per item, about 0.2 ms each. A `Float32Array` view should be a small, high-yield fix, and I'd run it as fix #4.
- **Row reads:** the HTML still lives in the `items` row, so every card read still pulls it off disk. The real fix is moving article HTML and text out of that row. That needs a migration, so I wouldn't do it this week.
- **Glass and runtime baseline:** the startup baseline, the edge-blur layers, and WebGPU glass costs all wait on your glass-fix PR.
- **Smaller items:** URL enrichment parsing HTML three times on the main thread, and fresh image cards showing the full original until the thumbnail lands.

My Windows port of the grid bench is still uncommitted in this worktree. I'll commit it separately once the glass fix merges and the click step is confirmed. SQU-15 stays In Progress.

Want me to run fix #4 (the vector decode) next?

content.thinking:
The user gave three pieces of feedback: for the Float32Array fix, get a separate SWE-2 opinion and pick the most logically sound option; for the row read changes, the user wants to loop in SWE-2 but needs clarification on what that actually means, so I should explain it; and for the smaller items like URL enrichment parsing and fresh image cards, get SWE-2's review on whether the current approach should actually be something else.

I'm planning to launch three delegate tasks: one evaluating decode/dot-product vector options with possible microbenchmarking in a scratch directory outside the repo, one doing read-only design exploration for the row-read changes given migration risk before alpha, and one reviewing whether the two smaller items need fixing at all. I'm leaning toward using max effort for the harder design task and high effort for the other two, since the user wanted to test different effort levels.

I'm also weighing how to isolate the work — worktrees for repo access, plan mode for the read-only tasks, and an accept-edits mode restricted to scratch scripts only for the benchmarking task, since it needs to actually run code but shouldn't touch repo files. I need to make sure each task description gives enough context, including the current branch state they'd be starting from.

For the design question, I'm digging into where html/text/extractedText are stored in the metadata JSON column, and whether reading card fields forces SQLite to traverse overflow pages because of column ordering — since created_at, updated_at, and archived come after the large metadata blob, selecting them may require walking the overflow chain, which could be a real cost worth investigating.

I'm weighing options: a separate item_content table, generated/virtual columns for card fields, a dedicated card_metadata column, or leaving it as-is — and I need to factor in migration risk before alpha, rollback safety, and whether FTS triggers index metadata/content since search depends on reaching article text through that path.

Then for the review items — URL enrichment parsing shared across main via ai-jobs, and the image fallback logic in libraryItem.ts — I want to assess whether these need fixing before alpha, what evidence supports that, and what a minimal fix would look like, especially weighing the tradeoff around instant caption.

I also want to explain the SQLite overflow page issue in plain terms: full article HTML/text sits in the same row as the metadata JSON, so even though the earlier fix stopped JS from receiving that payload, SQLite still has to read and parse it from disk whenever the row loads, so the real fix is splitting html/text into a separate item_content table keyed by item id that's only read when the article is opened.

For the user's "swarm this" request, since they're asking to parallelize design exploration rather than fully understanding the tradeoffs yet, I think the right move is to explain the migration cost clearly first, then kick off a cheap read-only design study now while leaving the actual implementation decision for after they've seen the explanation.

That gives me three delegates total running in parallel at effort levels high/max/high, with Devin treated as an independent second opinion rather than a confirmation check. I'll write each prompt concisely but self-contained, including the measured numbers and relevant file references.

content.text:
I'll answer your second note here and send the other two to fresh Devin runs.

**Moving the HTML out of the item's row, in plain terms.** Every saved item is one row in SQLite's `items` table. For an article, the full cleaned HTML and plain text, often tens to hundreds of kB, are stored inside the `metadata` column of that same row. SQLite keeps big values in overflow pages chained off the row, and it still reads them whenever it touches that row. The grid and search only need the title, thumbnail and a few fields. Fix #2 stops JavaScript from receiving the article text, but SQLite still reads it off disk on every card read. The fix is a separate table, say `item_content`, keyed by item id, that is read only when you open the article or index it for search. The costs are migrating every user's existing library right before alpha, and reworking the search index, which currently reads `metadata`. That is why I'd treat it as a design question first, and I'm sending it out as a read-only study.

input.title: SQU-15 second opinion: vector decode (Devin high)
input.task:
You are giving an independent second opinion on a performance fix in inkling (Electron + SQLite, Windows desktop app). Read AGENTS.md at the repo root first; it values simple software over impressive machinery. Do NOT edit, create, delete, or commit any file inside the repo. You may write throwaway scripts ONLY under your OS temp directory, outside the repo, to measure things.

## Context
`electron/storage/search.ts` scores semantic search and similar-item search by decoding every stored embedding BLOB (768 float32 values, little-endian) and dot-producting it against a query vector, on the Electron main-process event loop, on every debounced keystroke. Current code:

```ts
function decodeFloatVector(blob: Uint8Array | null, dimension: number) {
  if (!blob || blob.byteLength !== dimension * 4) return null;
  const bytes = Buffer.from(blob.buffer, blob.byteOffset, blob.byteLength);
  return Array.from({ length: dimension }, (_, index) => bytes.readFloatLE(index * 4));
}
function dotProduct(left: ArrayLike<number>, right: ArrayLike<number>) { /* plain loop */ }
```
Measured: scoring costs roughly 0.2 ms of CPU per stored vector (about 220 ms per 1,000 vectors), so a 5,000-item library burns around a second of main-thread time per search. The query vector arrives from `embedQueryForSearch` in `electron/main.ts` and is passed through `searchItems(query, limit, queryVector)`.

My proposed fix: replace `decodeFloatVector` with a `Float32Array` view over the blob (copying only when `byteOffset % 4 !== 0`), keeping the same scoring. I want you to decide whether that is actually the best call.

## Your task
Form your own view; do not just confirm mine. Consider at least: (1) the Float32Array-view fix and its pitfalls (alignment, endianness, the Buffer pool, the driver returning shared or pooled buffers), (2) skipping the decode allocation entirely by dot-producting straight from the bytes, (3) anything that avoids rescanning every vector on every keystroke at all (for example caching decoded vectors in memory with invalidation on writes, or a prefilter) and whether it is worth its complexity for an alpha-scale library of a few thousand items, (4) any better alternative you find after reading the code (`electron/storage/search.ts`, `electron/embeddings.ts`, `electron/storage/spaces.ts`, `electron/embedding-contract.ts`). Read how embeddings are written (`storeEmbedding`) and used by Smart Spaces and `searchSimilar`.

Back every claim with evidence: write a small microbenchmark in your temp directory (use `bun`; measure `process.cpuUsage()` deltas rather than wall-clock because this machine is heavily loaded by other work; use at least 2,000 random 768-dim vectors and report min/median/max over several runs) comparing the current code with each option. Also demonstrate that the scores each option produces are bit-for-bit identical to the current code, or say exactly how and why they differ, since result ordering must not change. Do not run the app, Electron, or any dev server. Never kill processes by name or pattern.

## Report format
- Your recommendation in one sentence, then a table of options with measured CPU ms per 1,000 vectors, equivalence of scores (identical or not), complexity (lines and moving parts), and risk.
- The exact code you recommend (as a diff-style snippet in your reply, not applied to the repo).
- What you rejected and why. Anything in the current approach you think is wrong or fragile.
- How confident you are, and what you could not verify.
