input.title: SQU-15 design study: article content out of items row (Devin max)
input.task:
You are doing a READ-ONLY design study for inkling (Electron + SQLite, Windows desktop app) ahead of its first alpha release at the end of this week. Do not edit, create, delete, or commit any file; do not run builds, the app, Electron, or dev servers. Reading code and read-only commands (git log, grep) are fine. Read AGENTS.md at the repo root first; it values the smallest model that makes behavior unsurprising and warns against machinery that merely looks impressive. The main process uses Effect 4.

## The problem
Every saved item is one row in the `items` table (`electron/storage/schema.ts`). For articles, the cleaned HTML and plain text (often tens to hundreds of kB, in keys like `html`, `text`, `extractedText`, `safeEmbeds`) live inside that row's `metadata` JSON column, and `ocr_text` can also be large. A card read (library grid, search results, Space listings; see `electron/storage/shared.ts` card projection, `context.ts` `selectCards`, `items.ts` `listActiveItems`) only needs title, thumbnail path, a few allowlisted metadata fields and a `hasArticleContent` boolean. We already stopped JavaScript from receiving the article text by projecting it away in SQL, which gave about 2.6x less main-process CPU (for 1,000 items with ~40 kB html each: listActiveItems 937 ms to 359 ms), but SQLite still has to read and parse the big JSON from the row, and `listActiveItems` has no LIMIT. 359 ms of synchronous main-thread work per 1,000 items is still too much for a library that will grow.

## What I need from you
Decide whether and how to remove the heavy payload from the hot read path, and whether any of it is safe to do before an alpha that real users will install and keep their data in. Evaluate at least these options and any better one you find:
1. Status quo plus cheap tweaks: for example column order or a computed/stored small `card_metadata` column so card reads never touch `metadata`, a stored `has_article_content` flag, giving `listActiveItems` a limit or paging.
2. A new table (for example `item_content(item_id, html, text, extracted_text, ...)`) with a migration that moves existing data, with reads of article content going to the new table.
3. Storing the heavy content as files under `assets/items/<id>/` (the app already keeps assets beside the database).
4. Anything smaller or cleverer you find after reading the code.

Questions you must answer by reading the code, with file:line evidence:
- What reads `metadata.html`, `text`, `extractedText`, `safeEmbeds` today (reader, item detail, enrichment jobs, export/import in `export-library.ts` and `import-library.ts`, search, sanitizing)? Which would need to change for each option?
- How does search reach article text today? The FTS index and its triggers (`schema.ts`), `likeClause`, and the `items_fts` columns: does FTS index `metadata`? If article text moved, how would FTS, OCR text search and the LIKE fallback still find it? AGENTS.md lists article text search as a required path.
- How do migrations work here (`schema.ts` version handling), and what happens if a migration is interrupted or a user downgrades? Is the export/import format versioned, and would an old export still import? What would a rollback story look like for an alpha tester?
- SQLite facts you should verify or reason about carefully, not assume: how row storage and overflow pages behave when a later column (created_at, updated_at, archived come after metadata in the row) is read, and whether reordering or a separate small column actually avoids touching the overflow chain.

## Report format
- Your recommendation in two sentences, including a clear yes or no on "do this before the alpha".
- A comparison table: option, what it fixes (with an expected CPU effect you can justify), files it would touch, migration risk to existing user data, effort, rollback.
- If you recommend an option, a step-by-step minimal implementation plan with the exact files and the tests that would earn their place under AGENTS.md rules (migration and persistence tests count).
- Anything in the current schema or read paths that is fragile or wrong, found while reading.
- Your confidence and the things you could not verify without running code.

input.title: SQU-15 review: enrichment parsing + image fallback (Devin high)
input.task: You are reviewing two performance suspicions in inkling (Electron + React + SQLite, Windows desktop app) and deciding, honestly, whether either deserves to be fixed before the first alpha release at the end of this week. This is READ-ONLY: do not edit, create, delete, or commit any file; do not run builds, the app, Electron, or dev servers. Reading code and read-only commands (git log, grep) are fine. Read AGENTS.md at the repo root first, especially "What makes inkling special" (capture is instant, performance, quiet intelligence), the "taste" section, and "Fight scope creep". A finding that turns out not to matter is a perfectly good outcome; say so plainly. ## Suspicion 1: URL enrichment parses fetched HTML on the main thread An earlier audit claimed `src/lib/ingestion/url-ingestion.ts` (around lines 249-272) parses the fetched HTML up to three times (`parseDocument(rawHtml)` twice and once more after `sanitizeHtml`), plus Defuddle walking the DOM, all synchronously inside the `enrich_url` job that runs on the Electron main process (`electron/ai-jobs.ts` around lines 118-147), with responses up to 8 MB (a constant near line 31). The claim is that this stalls the main-process event loop, and therefore all IPC and the renderer, for an estimated 100-500 ms per captured article while the user keeps browsing. Verify or refute by reading the code end to end. Questions: are the parses really redundant or does each serve a different purpose? How big are real article pages in practice (reason from the 8 MB cap and typical pages)? Does anything in the pipeline already run in a worker or yield to the event loop? What is the smallest sensible fix if one is warranted (for example capping parsed bytes, removing a redundant parse, or a worker), and what would it risk for extraction quality (a URL with partial results must still beat an error card, per AGENTS.md)? How often does this run in realistic use (one capture at a time vs a bulk import of many links)? ## Suspicion 2: fresh image cards decode the original file until the thumbnail lands The earlier audit claimed `src/features/library/libraryItem.ts` (around lines 161-164) uses `item.thumbnailPath ?? (kind === "Image" ? item.localAssetPath : null)`, so a just-captured image card renders the untouched original (the app allows files up to 50 MB, see `electron/storage/items.ts` around line 201) until the `image_thumbnail` job finishes, and that a burst import or drag-drop of many photos decodes many multi-megapixel originals at once, causing scroll jank and a memory spike. There is a deliberate comment near lines 159-160 explaining the choice. The product requirement is that capture is instant and the card appears right away, so this tradeoff matters: showing the original immediately is part of why capture feels instant. Questions: what does the comment say and why was it chosen? How quickly does the thumbnail job normally run, and does the thumbnail worker run separately from slower jobs (look at `electron/main.ts` job setup, `electron/ai-jobs.ts`, `electron/thumbnail.ts`)? What does the grid do for `` loading (lazy, async decode, virtualization) so how many originals could realistically be decoded at once? Does the card re-render to the thumbnail automatically when it lands? Would any change risk the "card appears instantly" requirement? If a fix is warranted, what is the smallest one? ## Report format For each suspicion: a verdict of FIX BEFORE ALPHA, FIX LATER, or LEAVE ALONE; the evidence with file:line and quoted code; the realistic user-visible impact in plain words; and, only if you say fix, the smallest change and what test would earn its place. End with an overall ranking of the two by how much a real user would notice, and your confidence.

What is the smallest sensible fix if one is warranted (for example capping parsed bytes, removing a redundant parse, or a worker), and what would it risk for extraction quality (a URL with partial results must still beat an error card, per AGENTS.md)? How often does this run in realistic use (one capture at a time vs a bulk import of many links)? ## Suspicion 2: fresh image cards decode the original file until the thumbnail lands The earlier audit claimed `src/features/library/libraryItem.ts` (around lines 161-164) uses `item.thumbnailPath ?? content.text:
I'll answer your second note here and send the other two to fresh Devin runs.

**Moving the HTML out of the item's row, in plain terms.** Every saved item is one row in SQLite's `items` table. For an article, the full cleaned HTML and plain text, often tens to hundreds of kB, are stored inside the `metadata` column of that same row. SQLite keeps big values in overflow pages chained off the row, and it still reads them whenever it touches that row. The grid and search only need the title, thumbnail and a few fields. Fix #2 stops JavaScript from receiving the article text, but SQLite still reads it off disk on every card read. The fix is a separate table, say `item_content`, keyed by item id, that is read only when you open the article or index it for search. The costs are migrating every user's existing library right before alpha, and reworking the search index, which currently reads `metadata`. That is why I'd treat it as a design question first, and I'm sending it out as a read-only study.

input.title: SQU-15 second opinion: vector decode (Devin high)
input.task:
You are giving an independent second opinion on a performance fix in inkling (Electron + SQLite, Windows desktop app). Read AGENTS.md at the repo root first; it values simple software over impressive machinery. Do NOT edit, create, delete, or commit any file inside the repo. You may write throwaway scripts ONLY under your OS temp directory, outside the repo, to measure things.

## Context
`electron/storage/search.ts` scores semantic search and similar-item search by decoding every stored embedding BLOB (768 float32 values, little-endian) and dot-producting it against a query vector, on the Electron main-process event loop, on every debounced keystroke. Current code:

```ts
function decodeFloatVector(blob: Uint8Array | null, dimension: number) {
  if (!blob || blob.byteLength !== dimension * 4) return null;
  const bytes = Buffer.from(blob.buffer, blob.byteOffset, blob.byteLength);
  return Array.from({ length: dimension }, (_, index) => bytes.readFloatLE(index * 4));
}
function dotProduct(left: ArrayLike<number>, right: ArrayLike<number>) { /* plain loop */ }
```
Measured: scoring costs roughly 0.2 ms of CPU per stored vector (about 220 ms per 1,000 vectors), so a 5,000-item library burns around a second of main-thread time per search. The query vector arrives from `embedQueryForSearch` in `electron/main.ts` and is passed through `searchItems(query, limit, queryVector)`.

My proposed fix: replace `decodeFloatVector` with a `Float32Array` view over the blob (copying only when `byteOffset % 4 !== 0`), keeping the same scoring. I want you to decide whether that is actually the best call.

## Your task
Form your own view; do not just confirm mine. Consider at least: (1) the Float32Array-view fix and its pitfalls (alignment, endianness, the Buffer pool, the driver returning shared or pooled buffers), (2) skipping the decode allocation entirely by dot-producting straight from the bytes, (3) anything that avoids rescanning every vector on every keystroke at all (for example caching decoded vectors in memory with invalidation on writes, or a prefilter) and whether it is worth its complexity for an alpha-scale library of a few thousand items, (4) any better alternative you find after reading the code (`electron/storage/search.ts`, `electron/embeddings.ts`, `electron/storage/spaces.ts`, `electron/embedding-contract.ts`). Read how embeddings are written (`storeEmbedding`) and used by Smart Spaces and `searchSimilar`.

Back every claim with evidence: write a small microbenchmark in your temp directory (use `bun`; measure `process.cpuUsage()` deltas rather than wall-clock because this machine is heavily loaded by other work; use at least 2,000 random 768-dim vectors and report min/median/max over several runs) comparing the current code with each option. Also demonstrate that the scores each option produces are bit-for-bit identical to the current code, or say exactly how and why they differ, since result ordering must not change. Do not run the app, Electron, or any dev server. Never kill processes by name or pattern.

## Report format
- Your recommendation in one sentence, then a table of options with measured CPU ms per 1,000 vectors, equivalence of scores (identical or not), complexity (lines and moving parts), and risk.
- The exact code you recommend (as a diff-style snippet in your reply, not applied to the repo).
- What you rejected and why. Anything in the current approach you think is wrong or fragile.
- How confident you are, and what you could not verify.

input.title: SQU-15 design study: article content out of items row (Devin max)
input.task:
You are doing a READ-ONLY design study for inkling (Electron + SQLite, Windows desktop app) ahead of its first alpha release at the end of this week. Do not edit, create, delete, or commit any file; do not run builds, the app, Electron, or dev servers. Reading code and read-only commands (git log, grep) are fine. Read AGENTS.md at the repo root first; it values the smallest model that makes behavior unsurprising and warns against machinery that merely looks impressive. The main process uses Effect 4.

## The problem
Every saved item is one row in the `items` table (`electron/storage/schema.ts`). For articles, the cleaned HTML and plain text (often tens to hundreds of kB, in keys like `html`, `text`, `extractedText`, `safeEmbeds`) live inside that row's `metadata` JSON column, and `ocr_text` can also be large. A card read (library grid, search results, Space listings; see `electron/storage/shared.ts` card projection, `context.ts` `selectCards`, `items.ts` `listActiveItems`) only needs title, thumbnail path, a few allowlisted metadata fields and a `hasArticleContent` boolean. We already stopped JavaScript from receiving the article text by projecting it away in SQL, which gave about 2.6x less main-process CPU (for 1,000 items with ~40 kB html each: listActiveItems 937 ms to 359 ms), but SQLite still has to read and parse the big JSON from the row, and `listActiveItems` has no LIMIT. 359 ms of synchronous main-thread work per 1,000 items is still too much for a library that will grow.

## What I need from you
Decide whether and how to remove the heavy payload from the hot read path, and whether any of it is safe to do before an alpha that real users will install and keep their data in. Evaluate at least these options and any better one you find:
1. Status quo plus cheap tweaks: for example column order or a computed/stored small `card_metadata` column so card reads never touch `metadata`, a stored `has_article_content` flag, giving `listActiveItems` a limit or paging.
2. A new table (for example `item_content(item_id, html, text, extracted_text, ...)`) with a migration that moves existing data, with reads of article content going to the new table.
3. Storing the heavy content as files under `assets/items/<id>/` (the app already keeps assets beside the database).
4. Anything smaller or cleverer you find after reading the code.

Questions you must answer by reading the code, with file:line evidence:
- What reads `metadata.html`, `text`, `extractedText`, `safeEmbeds` today (reader, item detail, enrichment jobs, export/import in `export-library.ts` and `import-library.ts`, search, sanitizing)? Which would need to change for each option?
- How does search reach article text today? The FTS index and its triggers (`schema.ts`), `likeClause`, and the `items_fts` columns: does FTS index `metadata`? If article text moved, how would FTS, OCR text search and the LIKE fallback still find it? AGENTS.md lists article text search as a required path.
- How do migrations work here (`schema.ts` version handling), and what happens if a migration is interrupted or a user downgrades? Is the export/import format versioned, and would an old export still import? What would a rollback story look like for an alpha tester?
- SQLite facts you should verify or reason about carefully, not assume: how row storage and overflow pages behave when a later column (created_at, updated_at, archived come after metadata in the row) is read, and whether reordering or a separate small column actually avoids touching the overflow chain.

## Report format
- Your recommendation in two sentences, including a clear yes or no on "do this before the alpha".
- A comparison table: option, what it fixes (with an expected CPU effect you can justify), files it would touch, migration risk to existing user data, effort, rollback.
- If you recommend an option, a step-by-step minimal implementation plan with the exact files and the tests that would earn their place under AGENTS.md rules (migration and persistence tests count).
- Anything in the current schema or read paths that is fragile or wrong, found while reading.
- Your confidence and the things you could not verify without running code.

Three Devin runs are going, all read-only apart from throwaway microbenchmarks in a temp folder. Nothing will be implemented until I've reviewed what they say.

| Run | Question | Level | Thread |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vector decode | Is a `Float32Array` view the best fix, or is there something better, such as skipping the decode or caching vectors? It has to prove its answer with CPU-time microbenchmarks and bit-identical scores. | high | <t3-thread://v2/8164cce9-439b-4404-a9e9-e2c2bccb629b/thread:delegated-task:command%3Amcp%3A07a26493-ec1e-4d0e-9e4c-aa3d1731bc4e%3Adelegate-task%3Afca0ea3d-fa54-4057-825c-c9f157e04dca> |
| Article content out of the row | Should heavy HTML and text leave the `items` row, and is any of it safe before the alpha? | max | <t3-thread://v2/8164cce9-439b-4404-a9e9-e2c2bccb629b/thread:delegated-task:command%3Amcp%3A07a26493-ec1e-4d0e-9e4c-aa3d1731bc4e%3Adelegate-task%3Ad41672aa-8280-4f12-8148-e4fab80469af> |
| The two smaller items | Do URL enrichment parsing and the image-card fallback deserve a fix, or should they be left alone? | high | <t3-thread://v2/8164cce9-439b-4404-a9e9-e2c2bccb629b/thread:delegated-task:command%3Amcp%3A07a26493-ec1e-4d0e-9e4c-aa3d1731bc4e%3Adelegate-task%3A02d88023-2e12-4cae-9c76-7c994b4d4beb> |

I wrote each brief to avoid steering them toward my own answer:
- **Vector decode:** it was told to form its own view and not just confirm mine.
- **Article content:** it must answer how search, export/import and migration rollback would change. Search over article text is a required path in your AGENTS.md, so it can't be broken.
- **The two smaller items:** "leave alone" is explicitly a fine verdict. For the image fallback, I flagged that showing the original instantly is part of why capture feels instant, so any fix must weigh that.

When they finish, I'll check their evidence against the code, then pick whatever is most sound and best supported. For fix #4 I'll also re-run my CPU-time comparison before I commit anything.

Both suspicions traced end to end; here's the report. ## Suspicion 1 — URL enrichment parses HTML on the main thread **Verdict: FIX LATER.** The mechanism is real, but the cost is a one-time ~0.1–0.5s hitch per article capture, with no bulk path to multiply it. **Evidence** - The "workers" are in-process queue-drain loops, not threads. `makeWorker` (`electron/storage/worker.ts:20-93`) runs processors as Effects forked on the main process — both the `main` and `thumbnails` lanes share the main event loop (`electron/main.ts:207-218`). Only `sqlite-snapshot-worker.ts` uses `worker_threads`, for DB snapshots. - `enrich_url` (`electron/ai-jobs.ts:140-147`) → `ingestUrl` (`src/lib/ingestion/url-ingestion.ts:239`). After the async fetch, all DOM work is synchronous and uninterruptible — Effect timeouts only fire at async boundaries. - The two full-page `parseDocument(rawHtml)` calls (`url-ingestion.ts:249-250`) are **not redundant**: `extractionDocument` is mutated by `promoteInfoAsides` (251) and Defuddle (`useAsync:false, standardize:true`, `defuddle-adapter.ts:25-30`); `sourceDocument` must stay pristine for `extractFallback` (252), `visibleByline` (265), `collectImageUrls` (287), `collectSafeEmbeds` (316). - There are actually *more* parses than the audit counted, but on the smaller extracted content, not the page: `sanitizeHtml` re-parses (`html-safety.ts:269`), `contentDocument` re-parses (271), and `hasReadableText`/`htmlToText` re-parse ~4 more times (260, 275, 313, and inside `mergeExtraction` at 43). - A blocked main loop stalls **all** IPC — `ipcMain.handle` commands *and* `protocol.handle("app")` asset streaming (`main.ts:530`, `asset-response.ts`), so card images loading concurrently stall too. - Frequency: one job per capture, sequential. Every capture path is single-URL (drop takes `files[0]`/first URL line, `useCapture.ts:504-515`; paste first file, 397; deep links one-per-event; extension server rate-limited 60/min). `import_library` restores rows, doesn't re-ingest. Bonus finding: the extension's `defuddledHtml` is validated then **discarded** — `handleRequest` only passes `{sourceUrl, title, captureSource}` (`capture-server.ts:681-687`), so extension captures also refetch and parse on main. **Impact:** save stays instant; seconds later the app can hitch once — a skipped scroll frame or a ~0.2s search keystroke lag. Typical article HTML is ~0.2–1 MB; the 8 MB cap (`url-ingestion.ts:31`, enforced while streaming at `http.ts:57-77`) is the pathological ceiling at ~1–3s. **Smallest fix when scheduled:** reorder `ingestUrl` to parse `rawHtml` once — run all read-only consumers first, then `promoteInfoAsides` + Defuddle on the same document last. Same output, ~halves the biggest cost, zero quality risk. Optionally stop re-parsing content for `hasReadableText` (260/275). A worker_thread is the "real" fix but new machinery — against the repo's taste rules. Do not fix by truncating `rawHtml` — head-truncation can cut the article body, and partial results must beat an error card. Test: extend the existing ingestion test asserting the fixture extracts identically with the shared document, not a new suite. ## Suspicion 2 — fresh image cards decode the original until the thumbnail lands **Verdict: LEAVE ALONE.** Deliberate, commented, and mitigated at every layer. - Comment at `libraryItem.ts:159-160`: *"…until it lands (or if it never can be) the card shows the original instead of a placeholder."* The fallback also covers thumbnails that can never be produced — removing it leaves those cards blank forever. - Thumbnails run on a dedicated lane (`thumbnailProcessors`, `ai-jobs.ts:267-287`; `main.ts:212` comment: *"New cards wait on thumbnails, so they never queue behind OCR or embeddings"*). Sharp resize ≈ 100–500ms. - Auto-swap confirmed: `jobs.notify` → `inkling:job-updated` (`main.ts:175-180`) → coalesced 400ms patch (`useLibraryData.ts:204-222`) → `item.image` becomes `thumbnail.webp`. - Concurrent decodes bounded: virtualized grid (`VirtuosoMasonry`, `LibraryStage.tsx:57`), `loading="lazy"` + `decoding="async"` on every card `` (`LibraryCard.tsx:222-224`), decode on renderer raster threads, not the main process. - Burst bounded at the source: drop/paste take only `files[0]` (`useCapture.ts:397,504`). Worst realistic case is ~a screenful of multi-MP originals for ~1–2s — a transient bitmap bump Chromium evicts under pressure. **Impact:** none attributable — the card shows the real image instantly (the intended UX) and quietly swaps to a small thumbnail a second later. ## Ranking 1. **Suspicion 1** — more noticeable: a real main-loop stall per article capture, occasionally a felt UI hitch. FIX LATER (single-parse reorder). 2. **Suspicion 2** — essentially invisible and intentional. LEAVE ALONE. **Confidence:** high on code facts (all verified end to end); medium on the millisecond estimates, reasoned from payload sizes and parser/decoder behavior rather than measured — benchmarking was out of scope.

content.text: The review of the two smaller items is back, and I agree with both verdicts after spot-checking the code. ## Image fallback (`libraryItem.ts`): leave alone The comment confirms it's deliberate: until the thumbnail lands, or if one can never be made, the card shows the original instead of a blank. That is part of why capture feels instant. Drop takes only the first file, the grid is virtualized, and every `` is lazy with async decode. Removing the fallback would leave cards blank forever where thumbnails fail. My earlier audit overstated this one, and I wouldn't touch it. ## URL enrichment parsing: fix later The mechanism is real. The "workers" run on the main process's event loop, so synchronous DOM work blocks all IPC and image streaming. But it's one article at a time, so the cost is a single hitch of roughly 0.1–0.5 s per capture, and it isn't something that multiplies. - **Two page parses:** the reviewer found the two full-page parses aren't redundant. One document is mutated by Defuddle, and the other must stay pristine for the fallback extractor. I confirmed both parses at the top of `ingestUrl`. - **Fix:** parse once, run all the read-only consumers first, then mutate the document last. That costs nothing in extraction quality. Truncating the HTML would not be safe, because it could cut the article body. A real worker thread would be new machinery the repo's taste rules argue against. - **Timing:** I'd leave it out of the alpha push and log it. I'll add it as a follow-up if you want it before the end of the week. The ordering change touches extraction, so it needs the existing ingestion tests as a guard. ## Something beyond performance The reviewer noticed that the Chrome extension sends the already-extracted page content, and the receiver validates it and then throws it away. Extension captures refetch the URL from the app instead. That wastes work, and it likely means a page behind a login, which the extension can see but the app can't, saves badly. You may want to check this. It's a product question, not part of this perf pass. I'm still waiting on the vector-decode and article-content runs.

# Second opinion: embedding decode in `electron/storage/search.ts`

**Recommendation in one sentence:** take the `Float32Array` view fix — it's the smallest possible change, produces bit-for-bit identical scores, is ~35× faster than the current decode under V8, and it already lands you at the performance floor that a decoded-vector cache would reach, so skip the cache entirely.

## Measured results

Benchmarked in my temp dir (`C:\Users\chris\AppData\Local\Temp\inkling-embed-bench.mjs`, `-fine.mjs`), 2,000 random 768-dim blobs, `process.cpuUsage()` deltas, min/median/max over 9 runs with each sample spanning 5 full scans (Windows quantizes CPU usage to ~15.6ms, so short loops need aggregation). Primary numbers under **Node 26 / V8** (the engine family Electron 45 ships; Bun/JSC included as a second data point):

| Option | CPU ms / 1,000 vectors (V8) | Scores vs current | Complexity | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A. Current `readFloatLE` + `Array.from` | 97 / 105 / 122 (you measured ~220 in-app) | — | status quo | allocates ~31MB transient per 5,000-row scan |
| **B. `Float32Array` view (+copy iff misaligned)** | **2.9** | **Object.is-identical, all 2,000** | ~5 lines, one function | host-endianness assumption (LE-only — always true on Windows) |
| C. Byte-wise `readFloatLE` dot, no decode | ~19 | identical, all 2,000 | ~7 lines, duplicates decode logic at both call sites | same endianness safety, slower |
| C2. Byte-wise `DataView.getFloat32` dot | 9.3 | identical, all 2,000 | ~7 lines | same |
| D. Decoded-vector cache (dot only = the floor) | 3.6 | identical | new Map, two-phase query, invalidation on `storeEmbedding`/delete | **not worth it — see below** |
| Bun/JSC (non-production engine) | A: ~14, B: ~6, all compressed | identical | — | JSC is not what Electron runs |

Equivalence proof: all options produced `Object.is`-identical scores on all 2,000 vectors (each element is the f64 rounding of a stored f32 — identical whether read via `readFloatLE`, `DataView`, or `Float32Array` load — and the dot product accumulates in f64 in the same order). Top-20 ordering identical. The misaligned-blob copy path in B verified correct against a deliberately offset `Uint8Array`.

**The decisive finding for option D:** a cache only eliminates the decode, and the view already makes the decode free. After fix B, the remaining ~3ms/1,000 *is* the dot product, which a cache still pays every keystroke. What a cache could additionally save is blob *materialization* — measured via `node:sqlite` (the actual driver: `@effect/sql-sqlite-node` wraps `DatabaseSync`, verified in `node_modules`): ~39ms to materialize 5,000 rows × 3KB blobs, vs ~28ms for a metadata-only scan. So the best a two-phase id/`created_at` diff + lazy blob fetch buys is ~11ms per keystroke on a 5,000-item library — nowhere near worth a `Map`, an extra query, and invalidation logic keyed on `item_embeddings.created_at`. Revisit only if libraries reach tens of thousands of items; at that point the ~28ms row-scan floor also needs attention (e.g., scoring in a worker thread or `sqlite-vec`).

## Recommended code

```ts
function decodeFloatVector(blob: Uint8Array | null, dimension: number) {
  if (!blob || blob.byteLength !== dimension * 4) return null;
  // Stored as little-endian float32; a view is valid because every host we ship
  // is little-endian. Copy only if a driver ever hands us an unaligned view.
  const aligned = blob.byteOffset % 4 === 0 ? blob : blob.slice();
  return new Float32Array(aligned.buffer, aligned.byteOffset, dimension);
}
```

Nothing else changes. `dotProduct` already takes `ArrayLike<number>`; the `vector.length !== queryVector.length` guards at both call sites still hold; `searchSimilar` gets the same speedup through the shared helper for free.

Pitfall checklist, verified rather than assumed:

- **Alignment:** `node:sqlite` returns a *fresh* `Uint8Array` per blob — I confirmed `byteOffset === 0` and `buffer.byteLength === blob.byteLength` on both full blobs and `substr()` slices under Node 26. `byteOffset % 4` will be 0 in practice; the `slice()` fallback costs 3 lines and covers any future driver returning views into shared buffers.
- **Endianness:** `readFloatLE`/`writeFloatLE` are endian-independent; a `Float32Array` view reads host-endian. Windows is always little-endian, so this is safe — but it's the one real semantic assumption, which is why the comment earns its place.
- **Buffer pool:** not applicable — `node:sqlite` doesn't pool; each row is a fresh allocation. Even if a driver pooled, the view is bounded by `byteOffset`/`byteLength` and is transient. One caveat worth remembering: *if* someone later caches these `Float32Array`s, views over pooled slabs would pin the whole slab — the copy-on-misalign path wouldn't protect against that.
- **Scores:** bit-for-bit identical, so result ordering cannot change.

## What I rejected, and what's fragile in the current code

- **Byte-wise dot (C/C2):** saves the decode allocation but keeps a per-element native call — 3–7× slower than the view under V8 (9.3–19 vs 2.9ms/1k), and it would fold decode+score into one function duplicated or reshaped at two call sites. Strictly worse than B on both axes.
- **Decoded-vector cache (D):** as shown, it's already at the same floor as B minus ~11ms of blob transfer per 5,000 rows. Two-phase queries plus invalidation on `storeEmbedding`'s `ON CONFLICT` update and cascade deletes is real machinery for nothing at alpha scale.
- **`sqlite-vec` / ANN index:** a new native dependency with Electron ABI packaging concerns to save a ~55ms/keystroke scan. Pure scope creep per "yagni".
- **What's actually fragile today:** the per-row `Buffer.from` wrapper + 768-element packed-double array is ~6.3KB of garbage per row — **~31MB of transient allocation per keystroke** on a 5,000-item library, which forces scavenges on the main thread. That GC pressure is likely why your in-app measurement (~220ms/1k) exceeds my synthetic decode number; fix B eliminates it entirely.
- **Post-fix bottleneck:** after B, the ~39ms SQL blob materialization becomes the dominant per-keystroke cost — worth knowing so nobody is surprised. Also note `embedQueryForSearch` runs ONNX inference per keystroke in `main.ts` (search.ts line 307) — likely comparable or larger than the entire post-fix scan; out of scope here, but the real "scan every vector every keystroke" cost is already bounded.

## Confidence

**High** on correctness and score equivalence (verified bit-for-bit, including the misaligned path) and on the cache-is-pointless conclusion (the math is structural, not measured). **Medium-high** on the absolute speedup in the real app: I benched Node 26's V8, not Electron 45's exact Node build, and real rows pass through Effect's row builder (which adds per-row cost to *both* current and fixed paths — it flatters neither). What I could not verify: Electron-runtime numbers, GC pause behavior in-app, and whether ~55ms/keystroke total at 5,000 items is the UX target you want — but it's ~20× better than today with 5 lines changed.

What a cache could additionally save is blob *materialization* — measured via `node:sqlite` (the actual driver: `@effect/sql-sqlite-node` wraps `DatabaseSync`, verified in `node_modules`): ~39ms to materialize 5,000 rows × 3KB blobs, vs ~28ms for a metadata-only scan. So the best a two-phase id/`created_at` diff + lazy blob fetch buys is ~11ms per keystroke on a 5,000-item library — nowhere near worth a `Map`, an extra query, and invalidation logic keyed on `item_embeddings.created_at`. Revisit only if libraries reach tens of thousands of items; at that point the ~28ms row-scan floor also needs attention (e.g., scoring in a worker thread or `sqlite-vec`).

## Recommended code

```ts
function decodeFloatVector(blob: Uint8Array | null, dimension: number) {
  if (!blob || blob.byteLength !== dimension * 4) return null;
  // Stored as little-endian float32; a view is valid because every host we ship
  // is little-endian. Copy only if a driver ever hands us an unaligned view.
  const aligned = blob.byteOffset % 4 === 0 ? blob : blob.slice();
  return new Float32Array(aligned.buffer, aligned.byteOffset, dimension);
}
```

Nothing else changes. `dotProduct` already takes `ArrayLike<number>`; the `vector.length !== queryVector.length` guards at both call sites still hold; `searchSimilar` gets the same speedup through the shared helper for free.

Pitfall checklist, verified rather than assumed:

- **Alignment:** `node:sqlite` returns a *fresh* `Uint8Array` per blob — I confirmed `byteOffset === 0` and `buffer.byteLength === blob.byteLength` on both full blobs and `substr()` slices under Node 26. `byteOffset % 4` will be 0 in practice; the `slice()` fallback costs 3 lines and covers any future driver returning views into shared buffers.
- **Endianness:** `readFloatLE`/`writeFloatLE` are endian-independent; a `Float32Array` view reads host-endian. Windows is always little-endian, so this is safe — but it's the one real semantic assumption, which is why the comment earns its place.
- **Buffer pool:** not applicable — `node:sqlite` doesn't pool; each row is a fresh allocation. Even if a driver pooled, the view is bounded by `byteOffset`/`byteLength` and is transient. One caveat worth remembering: *if* someone later caches these `Float32Array`s, views over pooled slabs would pin the whole slab — the copy-on-misalign path wouldn't protect against that.
- **Scores:** bit-for-bit identical, so result ordering cannot change.

## What I rejected, and what's fragile in the current code

- **Byte-wise dot (C/C2):** saves the decode allocation but keeps a per-element native call — 3–7× slower than the view under V8 (9.3–19 vs 2.9ms/1k), and it would fold decode+score into one function duplicated or reshaped at two call sites. Strictly worse than B on both axes.
- **Decoded-vector cache (D):** as shown, it's already at the same floor as B minus ~11ms of blob transfer per 5,000 rows. Two-phase queries plus invalidation on `storeEmbedding`'s `ON CONFLICT` update and cascade deletes is real machinery for nothing at alpha scale.
- **`sqlite-vec` / ANN index:** a new native dependency with Electron ABI packaging concerns to save a ~55ms/keystroke scan. Pure scope creep per "yagni".
- **What's actually fragile today:** the per-row `Buffer.from` wrapper + 768-element packed-double array is ~6.3KB of garbage per row — **~31MB of transient allocation per keystroke** on a 5,000-item library, which forces scavenges on the main thread. That GC pressure is likely why your in-app measurement (~220ms/1k) exceeds my synthetic decode number; fix B eliminates it entirely.
- **Post-fix bottleneck:** after B, the ~39ms SQL blob materialization becomes the dominant per-keystroke cost — worth knowing so nobody is surprised. Also note `embedQueryForSearch` runs ONNX inference per keystroke in `main.ts` (search.ts line 307) — likely comparable or larger than the entire post-fix scan; out of scope here, but the real "scan every vector every keystroke" cost is already bounded.

## Confidence

**High** on correctness and score equivalence (verified bit-for-bit, including the misaligned path) and on the cache-is-pointless conclusion (the math is structural, not measured). **Medium-high** on the absolute speedup in the real app: I benched Node 26's V8, not Electron 45's exact Node build, and real rows pass through Effect's row builder (which adds per-row cost to *both* current and fixed paths — it flatters neither). What I could not verify: Electron-runtime numbers, GC pause behavior in-app, and whether ~55ms/keystroke total at 5,000 items is the UX target you want — but it's ~20× better than today with 5 lines changed.

content.thinking:
Looking at the V8 numbers on Electron Node 24, searchSimilar went from 359 to 297 and hybrid from 1235 to 1046 — only around a 15% improvement, which falls within noise given the overlapping ranges between old and new runs. Devin's prediction of decode time dropping from 100ms to 3ms per 1000 vectors would suggest searchSimilar should fall closer to 260, but the observed ~60ms drop is smaller than expected, though the ranges do partially overlap.

This suggests the dominant remaining cost isn't decode at all — it's likely row materialization through Effect and SQL row creation overhead. So fix #4 is correct, tiny, and safe with identical scores, but the measured benefit here is modest (15-20%, noisy), not the dramatic 35x improvement Devin's microbenchmark implied; most of the real bottleneck lies in reading rows rather than decoding vectors. It's still worth keeping since it's a 4-line equivalent change that reduces GC pressure, but I need to be honest that my earlier "0.2ms per vector" estimate mischaracterized where the cost actually lives — it's mostly row transport, not vector decode.

Tracing this further, I suspect the real culprit is the items table scan itself: the join condition needs archived/kind/updated_at columns, and if archived and updated_at are positioned after the metadata column in storage order, SQLite has to traverse the overflow page chain for every one of those 1000 rows to reach them. With ~40KB per item row across 1000 rows, that's roughly 40MB of overflow page reads, which could easily account for the 200+ ms I'm seeing — this looks like the real source of the remaining cost, not decode or row transform.

I'll leave deeper verification to the design study rather than duplicating it, and settle on committing fix #4 with an updated changelog line clarifying that semantic search now scores stored vectors before loading full items, only fetching the matches it needs, and reads them without extra copying.

The Float32Array view optimization only gives a modest 15-20% speedup rather than the predicted gain, with overlapping ranges so it's not conclusively proven. I'll keep it anyway since it's safe, bit-identical, and reduces garbage collection overhead, and I'll document the real numbers honestly.

content.text:
Fix #4 is committed as `c3825c0`, and `check:changed` passes: oxlint, oxfmt, the storage tests, knip and typecheck.

## What the measurements showed
- **Under Bun**, which Devin's microbenchmark suggested was the wrong engine for this change, there was no gain. I had been benchmarking the wrong engine.
- **Under Electron's own V8**, the gain is about 15–20% on `searchSimilar` and hybrid search, and the ranges overlap. Devin's microbenchmark predicted about 35× on the decode alone. The decode itself probably is that much faster, but it was a small slice of the total cost.
- **I got one thing wrong earlier.** I attributed about 0.2 ms per item to the decode. Most of that was something else.

## What I think the real remaining cost is
This is a hypothesis, not yet proven. `searchSimilar` has to read each item's `archived`, `kind` and `updated_at` to filter and sort. Those columns sit after the huge `metadata` column in each row, so SQLite probably walks every row's overflow pages, about 40 kB each in my test library. That would explain why reading 1,000 rows costs hundreds of milliseconds no matter how fast the vector math is. If it holds, the fix is in the table layout: either a separate content table, or small card fields stored beside the key. The max-effort Devin study on the item row is the one that can settle this, and it was asked to check exactly that column-order question.

## Where things stand
- **Branch:** SQU-15 has four perf commits plus the changelog. Nothing is pushed and there's no PR.
- **Still running:** Devin's article-content study (max).
- **Waiting on you:** your glass-fix PR, before I can finish the Windows bench port and the startup baseline.
- **Parked:** the single-parse reorder for URL enrichment, which I'd do after the alpha push if you want it.

I'll let the content study finish before touching anything else in the storage layer.

The `item_content` split is implemented and fully verified. Summary of what landed:

**Schema (v8 → v9)** — `electron/storage/schema.ts`
- `item_content(item_id PK, html, text, extracted_text)` holds article payloads; `items.metadata` now carries only small fields.
- `migrateItemContent` moves `html`/`text`/`extractedText` out of existing metadata in one `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` txn — idempotent, retries next open, and degrades gracefully on failure (v8-shaped rows still work via fallbacks).
- `items_fts` gains `content_text`/`content_html`/`content_extracted_text`; FTS rows are keyed by `items.rowid` so deletes are O(1) instead of full-index scans, and items triggers fire only on `UPDATE OF` indexed columns — archive flips and thumbnail writes no longer rewrite FTS rows.
- `item_content` triggers rebuild the FTS row on insert/update/delete, so item-then-content ordering stays consistent in either direction.
- A rowid-drift check on open rebuilds the index if a future `VACUUM` ever reassigned live `items.rowid`s.

**Reads/writes**
- `shared.ts`: `splitItemMetadata` routes the three keys to content columns; `itemFromRow` merges them back so `getItem` returns the identical `StoredLibraryItemDetail` shape — renderer, `embeddingText`, and IPC are untouched.
- `cardColumnsFor` projects `hasArticleContent` via a header-only `EXISTS` probe (plus a legacy-metadata fallback), so card reads never touch the payload.
- All metadata write paths (`saveUrl`, `createNote`, `createQuote`, `saveFile`, `updateItem`, `applyUrlEnrichment`, `storeImagePalette`, `insertStaged` imports) funnel through split + `syncItemContent`; `deleteItem` removes the content row.
- LIKE fallback searches `item_content` via `EXISTS`; FTS path unchanged through the `item_id` join.
- `scripts/bench-library-grid.mjs` seeds the new layout so the benchmark stays truthful.

**Verification**
- `bun test electron/storage.test.ts` — 43/43 pass, including the new v8→v9 migration test (content moved, keys stripped, detail merged, html/text search via FTS, marker correct, delete cleans up, reopen idempotent).
- `ai-jobs`, `capture-server`, `video-poster` — 29/29 pass.
- `tsc-rs` electron typecheck, `oxlint`, `oxfmt`, `knip` — all clean.
- Changelog entry added under Unreleased → Changed (SQU-15).

One earlier timeout on the export/restore test was a machine-load flake — it passes at ~3.4s on rerun. Not committed; nothing pushed or PRed.

# inkling

inkling is a home for everything worth keeping. Articles, images, screenshots, PDFs, notes, quotes, video links. An Electron desktop app for Windows, with React, TypeScript, and Vite in the frontend and Node.js and SQLite in the backend. Everything stays on the machine.

Think of it as a private visual library with semantic search as the only organizer. No folders to maintain. Save arbitrary media in seconds, find it later by describing it.

## What makes inkling special

People keep things here they do not want to lose, things that are important to them, or that give them inspiration or creative ideas. These are the things that we must never compromise on.

### 1. Capture is instant and seamless

Saving must be faster than deciding where something belongs. The card appears right away. OCR, embeddings, fetching and/or indexing run in the background while the user keeps browsing or continues on with something else. A change that blocks capture on processing is a bug, no matter how correct the processing is.

### 2. Performance

Lots of apps have gotten bogged down with bad tech decisions and "slop". We regularly audit for performance regressions, often caused by passing full content over Electron IPC instead of summaries/thumbnails, rendering the card grid without virtualization, loading full assets where a thumbnail would do, blocking capture on extraction/OCR/embeddings, and running FTS + vector + Smart Space re-evaluation on every keystroke. Keep capture instant and processing in background jobs. Make sure all changes are considerate of performance impact.

### 3. Local first, forever

The library lives in SQLite on the user's disk, with files kept as assets beside it under `assets/items/<id>/`. No account, no feed, no tracking. Network is only for fetching data in a URL the user asked to save like video embed links, the one time model download, or when a user plays a video embed link but that is handled by the embed. Do not add calls home, analytics, or silent uploads.

### 4. Quiet intelligence

AI helpers stay invisible. They make search better. Never surface confidence scores, AI labels, tag correction flows, or model management chores in the main interface. Never rewrite a user title, note, or tag. When AI fails, fall back to plain metadata and text search. Our mascot is an ink-blot that stays out of the way. Calm at rest, subtly alive while work runs, sad only when capture fails. It never talks, never explains AI, never interrupts, it just chills in the background and gives some life to the app.

### 5. Visual by type

An article, a photo, a PDF, a quote and a note should not all look like generic bookmarks. Each media type gets its own card treatment and its own thumbnail. Keep it that way when adding types.

## A note on taste

Simple software that feels obvious beats impressive machinery. Do not preserve complexity just because it already exists. Do not introduce machinery because it looks architecturally impressive. Understand the real constraint, then fight for the smallest model that makes the correct behavior unsurprising.

Channel both "measure twice, cut once" and "yagni". Fight scope creep. Try to honor the dev's intent in both a minimal and realistic fashion.

The rest of this document is meant to help you navigate the codebase and make changes effectively. Think of these instructions less as "hard rules", more as "good defaults". The developer's preferences should be able to override anything here. Most work in this repo will be done by agents, sometimes remote. Be careful with data, dev servers, and anything that could damage the session you are working from.

If a rule here fights the task in front of you, say so plainly and get a human sign off before breaking it.

## Glossary

We need to be on the same page with terminology. When communicating, use this language:

- **you** means the agent reading this file and changing inkling.
- **we and maintainers** mean the people building inkling. That is who you are talking to now.
- **user** means the person using inkling, saving things and searching them later.
- **item** means one saved thing in the library, whatever its type. Data, not UI.
- **card** means how an item looks in the grid and in detail. UI, not data.
- **library** means the SQLite database plus the asset store on disk.
- **capture** means getting something into the library. Paste a URL, pick a file, drag in, paste from clipboard, screenshot, or deep link.
- **job** means one unit of background work. OCR, extraction, embeddings, indexing. Runs on a persisted queue with leases.
- **embedding** means the local vector for text or image search. Nomic text and vision share one 768-dimension space.
- **Space** means a saved search shown as a collection. Smart Spaces update themselves. Regular Spaces hold manually user curated items.
- **deep link** means the companion path into the app, `inkling://capture?url=...`.
- **preview** means `bun run dev`, the web-only look with sample data.
- **full app** means the Windows Electron desktop app with the real library, built with `bun run build:dir` or `bun run build:installer`.

## The three ways to hurt yourself

1. **Killing by pattern.** Never `pkill -f`, `pgrep | kill`, or `kill` a PID you found by matching a name, path, or worktree string. Your own agent process has this worktree's path in its argv, and this machine runs several other dev servers at once. Kill only a PID you captured at spawn, or the owner of your port after confirming it is your worktree (`Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort <port> -State Listen` and the `Win32_Process` command line on Windows, `ss -H -ltnp` and `/proc/<pid>/cwd` on Linux).

2. **Writing to the live library.** The developer's real data is the SQLite file and asset store the running app owns. Reading it is fine. Copying from it for test fixtures is good. Never start a server against it, never open it read-write, never clean it up.

3. **Baking in local paths and ports.** Never hardcode a localhost port, an absolute user path, or a machine specific model cache path into source or committed config. Preview and the full app must keep working from a fresh clone on another Windows machine. Never commit a database file, a model artifact, a downloaded embedding, or a benchmark output besides the two tracked files. Never commit a pairing secret, token, or full capture URL with real content.

## Hit every surface

The common defect here is a change that works on the path tested and is missing everywhere else. Before calling ingestion or display work done, walk this list and name the entries that applied; skip the rest silently.

- **Entry points.** A behavior reachable from the Add button is usually also reachable from paste, drag and drop, clipboard, screenshot capture, and the deep link. Fixing one is not fixing the feature.
- **Capture paths.** URL, article extraction, image file, screenshot, PDF, note, quote, video link, X post, misc file. An extractor change needs a decision per path, even if the decision is not supported here.
- **Search paths.** Titles, notes, article text, OCR text, domains, authors, manual tags, derived concepts, colors, semantic similarity, dates, types. If you index a new field, say how search reaches it.
- **Card types.** Article, image, PDF, video, post, note, quote, and file, as the `ItemKind` union in `src/lib/types.ts`. Shared thumbnail logic lives in one place. Keep the set coherent.
- **Reverse states.** If you added a way in, add the way out and a way to see it. Trash needs restore. A Space needs rename and delete that keeps its items. A one way door is a bug.
- **App modes.** Preview and the full app behave differently. OCR, embeddings, and file access only run in the Electron app. Do not ship a feature that silently does nothing in one mode.
- **Docs.** Check whether the change makes existing guidance inaccurate. Apply the [documentation rules](#documentation) before adding anything.

## Dev servers

- `bun install` installs. If module resolution looks broken, run `bun run check:bun-version`.
- `bun run dev` is the quick web look at the UI. It uses sample data and has no desktop storage or processing backend.
- `bun run dev:app` opens the Electron shell in preview mode. The renderer shows the sample library and does not call the desktop backend, so capture, OCR, embeddings, and local file access are not exercised there. Test the full backend with the packaged output of `bun run build:dir`.
- `t3.json` lists the T3 Code run scripts. Keep it up to date: whenever a package.json script is renamed or removed, or a command it runs changes, update `t3.json` in the same change.
- Ports and state come from the dev setup, not from memory. Read the actual terminal output. Do not assume a port.
- Stop what you started, by the handle you tracked. See rule 1.
- Never `Start-Sleep` (or any blocking wait) after launching a server. Start it detached, do other work, then poll its log or port. A sleep blocks you from doing anything else while you wait.

## Test data

An empty library is a bad test. Seed your run with a copy of real data instead of pointing at live state.

- Copy the database file with SQLite backup semantics so the copy is consistent even if the source app is open. A raw file copy of a live database is a corrupt copy. Bring the `-wal` and `-shm` siblings when you copy raw, or better, back up through the engine.
- Data flows one way. Into your sandbox, never back out. Copy in, never symlink. Never write your test edits back to the source.
- Bring assets only for the items your flow needs. Do not copy the whole asset store to test one card.
- The committed demo seed in `public/seed-demo/` plus `src/seedPersonal.ts` is the safe default for UI work. It shuffles with a fixed seed so the order is mixed but stable. Prefer it over real data when it covers your case.
- Never commit a copied database, a real user item, or a downloaded model. The gitignore already excludes run artifacts. Keep it that way.

## Verifying

- Smallest proof that the change works. While iterating, `bun test <files>` for the tests you touched. Before pushing, `bun run check:changed`: lint, format, tests, Knip, and typecheck scoped to what the branch changed. The full check is `bun run check`, which mirrors the CI frontend job. Do not run it unless you changed something broad or the user asked.
- **Do not run repo-wide checks.** No full `bun test` sweep or full `tsc` unless asked. CI owns the full suite.
- A test earns its place by guarding something that breaks quietly: extraction and sanitizing, embed allowlists, OCR scoring, queue leases and recovery, migrations and persistence, asset path containment and range requests, deep link and external-format parsing, ordering and race guarantees, and `liquidGlassShape`. A test added with a bug fix stays; mark it `// regression: #NNN` if its name doesn't say so.
- Don't write tests the types already prove, trivial logic, basic DOM behavior, static-markup renders, mock-call mirrors, smoke tests, duplicate table rows, or wall-clock and perf asserts.
- Ingestion and background changes ship with focused tests for that behavior. A behavior change with no test is unfinished.
- Proof for a bug fix depends on the bug. Logic, data, state, and protocol bugs get a failing test first (the fewest that fail on `main` for that reason), then the fix. Purely visual bugs (spacing, colour, alignment, a layout shift) get before/after captures and no test.
- Extend before you add. When an existing test or table covers the behavior, add a row or an assertion there. Write a new `it` only when no case fits. Test at the lowest layer that fails on `main`, not again in a wrapper or at each call site.
- Background work is async. Await the real signal: a job drain, a lease state, an event. No fixed sleeps, per-test timeouts, retries, `Date.now()` or `performance.now()` deltas, polling loops, or skips without a reason.
- UI changes need one real pass in the running app before you call them done (the `verify-inkling` skill drives it). Preview for layout, full app for anything native. Take a screenshot through the harness so the user can see it. The primary agent does this once after integrating. Subagents do not launch their own dev servers. Clean up what you launched when you are done.
- There are no local hooks. CI runs the frontend checks and Electron package smoke tests.

## Pull requests

- Never make a PR unless the developer explicitly asks you to do so.
- Conventional commit titles, plain language: `fix(reader): code blocks keep line breaks`.
- Body: the problem in a sentence or two, then how you fixed it. End with the model and harness that did the work.
- UI changes need before/after images. Motion or timing needs a short video.
- Upload PR evidence to GitHub. Never commit PR-only screenshots or assets such as `.github/pr-assets/`.
- One request is one PR. Split it only when the maintainer asks.

## Linear issues

- One Linear issue owns one task (e.g. `SQU-6`). That issue is the tracker, not a plan file.
- Before starting: read the issue + comments, move it to In Progress, branch from its `gitBranchName`.
- While working: post major progress as issue comments, never rewrite the description. Keep scratch outside the worktree.
- Monitor by reading status + comments only. Don't start work on an issue already In Review unless asked.
- Before finishing: link the PR to the issue at the top of the description before all content, move it to In Review, tick the `roadmap.md` box and add a changelog line referencing the issue ID in the same PR.
- If merged: move the issue to Done.

## Documentation

Most code changes need no docs change. Agents can read the code.

- Product intent lives in `docs/product.md` and `docs/product-behavior.md`. Architecture reasons live in `docs/tech-stack.md`. Standing goes in `docs/roadmap.md`. What changed goes in `docs/changelog.md`. Do not invent a second place for the same fact.
- Before adding a paragraph, ask what a maintainer would get wrong without it. If reading the relevant code answers the question, leave it out.
- Do not document every feature, enumerate fields or methods, narrate control flow, maintain file catalogs, or append PR summaries. Types, tests, and code already record the implementation. The glossary defines shared vocabulary; it is not a feature index.
- Keep a local implementation explanation in a nearby code comment. Use an internal doc when the reasoning crosses boundaries or needs context the code cannot carry well. Link to the relevant source instead of copying it.
- When a documented decision or constraint changes, rewrite or remove the affected text. Do not append another account of the new behavior. A new internal page needs a distinct, durable reason to exist.
- Keep user docs in the shipped product's voice, without implementation details or contributor tooling. Update the relevant feature section when how to use it changes. A UI tweak does not need a documentation entry, and a new control does not need its own page. A settings path is useful; descriptions of visible buttons, icons, layouts, animations, or every UI state are not. Before adding text, ask what task or decision it helps the user with.
- The changelog rules live at the top of `docs/changelog.md` and still apply. One line per entry, grouped under Added, Changed, Fixed, Removed, Deprecated, Security. Trivial edits skip the changelog.
- `docs/operations/` holds maintainer setup, release, and debugging procedures. Keep instructions for operating an installed inkling version in the user guides.

## Plans and work artifacts

- Do not commit implementation plans, research notes, or agent scratch files. Keep temporary working material outside the worktree. `.plans/` is gitignored only as a safety net for legacy tooling.
- Track active maintainer work in its Linear issue (see [Linear issues](#linear-issues)). External proposals follow `CONTRIBUTING.md`.
- A merged PR is the implementation record. Do not keep a task checklist in the repository; `docs/roadmap.md` records milestone standing only.

## How it works

Capture creates the item immediately, then background jobs do the slow parts. Normalize, extract text and metadata, run OCR or PDF extraction or article parsing, generate embeddings. Writes to items update the FTS index through triggers. The user keeps browsing or does something else while jobs run. A job can be retried, its lease can expire, and interrupted jobs recover on restart.

Search combines exact FTS over content, notes, and OCR text with semantic similarity over local embeddings. Smart Spaces are saved searches whose query runs each time their items load, so they need no background job.

The Electron main process owns files, the job queue, the database, and model execution. It is written with Effect 4, whose API differs a lot from the Effect 3 most models remember. Before writing or changing Effect code, read `node_modules/effect/AGENTS.md`, `node_modules/effect/ai-docs/`, and the package source instead of relying on memory (run `bun install` if `node_modules` is missing). The renderer gets a narrow preload bridge, not raw filesystem or shell access. Fetched HTML is untrusted. It gets sanitized, embeds pass an allowlist, scripts and event handlers are stripped.

Full reasoning in `docs/tech-stack.md`. Behavior contract in `docs/product-behavior.md`.

## Where code lives

- `src/` is the React and TypeScript frontend. Entry at `src/main.tsx`. Feature code lives in `src/features/` by area (library, item-view, spaces, capture, shell, settings). `src/App.tsx` composes the features, and the reader is `src/ReaderView.tsx`.
- `src/lib/ingestion/` is the capture and extraction pipeline. Defuddle, metadata fallback, sanitizing, video link handling. URL ingestion also runs in Electron's main process (`electron/ai-jobs.ts` imports it).
- `src/components/` holds shared pieces such as the card media (`ItemMedia.tsx`), the liquid glass surfaces, the mascot, and onboarding. `src/ui/` holds shared UI primitives.
- `packages/contracts/` is the IPC contract: the command list and Effect Schemas that preload, main, and renderer share. The renderer calls them through `src/lib/libraryApi.ts`.
- `packages/ingestion-shared/` is the capture payload format and validation shared by the extension and the app.
- `electron/` holds the desktop main process (`main.ts`), preload bridge, PDF/OCR, embeddings, the loopback capture receiver (`capture-server.ts`), and packaging inputs. SQLite schema, storage, and the job queue are in `electron/storage/`.
- `extension/` is the Chrome extension, a capture entry point. It posts to the loopback receiver, or hands the URL to the app through the `inkling://capture` link.
- `scripts/` holds build and check scripts, such as `build-electron.ts` and `assert-command-refs.ts`.
- `benchmarks/` holds the corpus, the harness, expected outputs, and results. Of `benchmarks/results/`, only `results-latest.json` and `summary.md` are tracked.
- `public/seed-demo/` plus `src/seedPersonal.ts` is the committed demo library for UI work.
- `docs/` holds product, behavior, design, models, stack, roadmap, bugs, and changelog. Maintainer procedures live in `docs/operations/`, and `docs/README.md` indexes them.

## Taste

- Complexity belongs at the adapter boundary. Ingestion stays explicit, UI stays dumb.
- Inferred types over annotations. `any` is the enemy.
- Effect lives in the main process and stops at the IPC edge. The one renderer use is `src/lib/ingestion/http.ts` (preview-mode capture); don't add more. Reusable Effect functions use `Effect.fnUntraced`, not `Effect.fn` (nothing collects spans). Keep `Effect.gen` for inline programs and layers.
- Default to no comment. Keep one only where a reader would likely break something without it: a race or ordering guarantee, a security or sanitizing check, a Chromium, Electron, WebGPU or OS quirk, or an invariant another file relies on. One line where you can, four at most. Don't restate names, narrate steps, label sections, record history, explain the fix you just made (the PR carries that), or leave a TODO without an issue. Lint directives, knip tags and license headers stay. `inkling/no-low-value-comments` in `oxlint-plugin-inkling/` enforces the length cap and the mechanical cases, and every `oxlint-disable` needs a `-- reason`.
- Our users should never notice a dropped frame, a lying spinner, and a stale label. No continuously repainting animations (with a slight exception for the mascot); they peg the GPU on high-refresh displays.
- Capture paths stay fast and forgiving. Keep partial results when extraction fails. A URL with a title and domain beats an error card.

## Additional tips

- Security is important, but should not be over-indexed on, especially for dev mode/maintainer-only features. The main threat is untrusted web content rendered locally; `docs/tech-stack.md` says to treat all fetched HTML as untrusted. Keep sanitizing and allowlists strict. Keep dev ergonomics simple.

- [No counters on onboarding mockups](onboarding-mockups-no-chrome.md) — Paper onboarding designs show only what the app would show; no "01 / 04" step counters
- [Onboarding flow direction](onboarding-flow-direction.md) — screen order, favourite screens, mascot big-small-small-big rhythm and peek/eyes ideas
- [Alpha crash reporting decision](alpha-crash-reporting-decision.md) — PostHog crash reports approved, opt-out, US region; overrides the no-telemetry rule for alpha
